meta_description: Agents earn autonomy in tiers: what they may do alone, with approval, never.

blocks.x: Agents earn autonomy in tiers: what they may do alone, with approval, never.

The policy envelope is the product is not a slogan; it is a delivery position. The evidence is consistent across industries — the constraint is rarely technology; it is whether the operating model takes this seriously from sprint one.

items: Autonomy granted without policy is liability; policy without telemetry is fiction.
Replay evaluation on historical cases catches the 20% variance that breaks scripts.
Escalation design is where agent programs win or lose operator trust.

blocks.x: Three questions to ask your current vendors

items: What is the classical baseline every proposed capability must beat, measured on identical data?
Who signs the go/no-go gate, and what evidence do they require before signing?
What did you stop last quarter, and what did the stop save us?

blocks.x: Programs stall when the operating model is treated as an afterthought — the technology works in week six and the organization has not changed in week sixty, so the capability quietly degrades into shelfware.

items: falsifiable criteria and locked baselines before build; the demo is the least important artifact.
named owners, run models and escalation paths agreed with the operating team, not for it.
replay trails, control tests and documentation as artifacts of the build — never reconstructed.

blocks.x: Mature agent fleets run above 85% task-slot utilization with sub-minute rollbacks.
